claim: The number of active English Wikipedia editors (>=5 edits/month) grew until early 2007, then abruptly stopped growing and entered a steady linear decline.
stance_target: Wikipedia's contributor base has a documented, dated inflection point after which aggregate participation declines
quoted_support: the number of active editors (editors with >= 5 edits/month) abruptly stopped growing in early 2007 and entered a steady, linear decline.

claim: Wikipedia's editor-retention decline is attributable specifically to falling retention of new editors, not to a decline in the retention rate of already-experienced editors.
stance_target: the mechanism of Wikipedia's participation decline is a newcomer-retention problem, not a veteran-attrition problem
quoted_support: Recent research has shown evidence that this transition is rooted in the declining retention of new editors, not a change in the retention of already-experienced old-timers.

claim: Wikipedia's newcomer-survival metric is operationally defined as the proportion of desirable (good-faith/golden) newcomers who go on to edit for at least two months.
stance_target: operational definition of editor retention used in the canonical Wikipedia decline literature
quoted_support: Survival of desirable newcomers. The proportion of desirable newcomers who edit for at least two months is plotted over time.

claim: Editors who revert newcomer contributions using the semi-automated tool Huggle engage in the recommended Bold-Revert-Discuss follow-up discussion only about 7% of the time, versus about 60% for editors who revert manually.
stance_target: automated/semi-automated quality-control tools contribute to newcomer attrition by depersonalizing rejection
scope_conditions: English Wikipedia, reverts via Huggle vs. manual reverts
quoted_support: editors who revert using Huggle are much less likely to participate in a BRD discussion (~7%) than editors who revert manually (~60%).
